title: Content Analysis of COVID-19 Vaccine and Infertility Tweets: The Etiology of a Misinformation Pandemic
screen_reason: Content analysis of tweets containing both a COVID-19-vaccination term and a fertility term, coded factual vs misinformation; the abstract reports the share of such tweets that were misinformation at two time points (29.9% July 2021, 45.1% December 2021). That is a quantitative share of items judged false against a factuality standard, so CONTENT. The item is a published conference abstract (MRSi Abstracts, North American Proceedings in Gynecology & Obstetrics), i.e. there is no fuller text to recover; denominators, coder identity and reliability are therefore unavailable.

estimates.country: Not stated (public Twitter dataset; misinformation rates compared with US COVID-19 case counts)
estimates.date: Two collection windows: July 2021 and December 2021
estimates.measure_type: % of COVID-19-vaccine-and-fertility tweets classified as misinformation (December 2021 window; representative point of the two-point series)
estimates.denominator: Relevant tweets from a public dataset containing at least one COVID-19-vaccination word and one fertility word, in the December 2021 window (number not reported in the abstract)
estimates.definition: Tweet analysed for factuality and classified into the misinformation group rather than the factual group
estimates.misinfo_def: Not defined beyond the factual vs misinformation contrast: "Relevant tweets were analyzed for factuality."
estimates.source_quote: RESULTS: Misinformation tweets rose from 29.9% in July 2021 to 45.1% in December 2021.
estimates.page_loc: Abstract, RESULTS (MRSi Conference Abstracts, Summer 2022, p. 5)
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Not reported: the abstract states only that 'Relevant tweets were analyzed for factuality'; no coder count, codebook, external fact-check source or reliability statistic is given
estimates.moderator_quote: Tweets included were from key points in the COVID19 vaccine discourse (July 2021 and December 2021) and contained at least one word related to COVID19 vaccination and one word related to fertility.
estimates.notes: Two-point series collapsed to one row per the time-series rule; the December 2021 (later) point is used as the representative value and the July 2021 value (29.9%) is recorded verbatim in value_raw so an adjudicator can substitute it. Confidence is medium, not high: the abstract gives no denominator size and no coding procedure or reliability, so the value cannot be audited. Country coded Global for want of any stated geography, though comparison to US case counts suggests a US-centric dataset.

missed_or_uncertain: Nothing further is extractable: the source is a one-page conference abstract. Not extracted - (a) the correlations with daily US COVID-19 case counts (r=-0.50; r=0.53), which are associations, not shares; (b) follower/verification/engagement/sentiment comparisons, which are group differences with no misinformation share; (c) hashtag lists. No denominator counts, sample size, coder details or reliability statistics are reported anywhere in the text, so the two values cannot be checked against raw counts, and no per-country or per-definition split is available.

rob.design: Content analysis of a public Twitter dataset restricted to two purposive windows (July 2021, December 2021) and to tweets containing at least one COVID-19-vaccination word and one fertility word; tweets coded factual vs misinformation with no reported codebook, coder count or inter-rater reliability; no sample size reported; group comparisons by ANOVA/chi-square; conference-abstract reporting only, so most risk-of-bias items are unassessable.
rob.item6_quote: Relevant tweets were analyzed for factuality.
rob.item10_quote: Misinformation tweets rose from 29.9% in July 2021 to 45.1% in December 2021.
